title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Grothendieck sets up variants of the relative Picard functor whose objects are line bundles carrying a connection. Let f: X → S be a morphism and f^{fl} the induced morphism of fppf sites.

(1) P^c_{X/S} is the fppf sheaf associated to the presheaf sending S' to the isomorphism classes of invertible sheaves on X_{S'} with a connection relative to S'. Forgetting the connection gives the exact sequence (1.1):
0 → f_*Ω^1_{X/S} / dlog(f_*O_X^*) → P^c → Pic_{X/S} → R^1 f_*Ω^1_{X/S}.
- The kernel is the torsor of connections on the trivial bundle, modulo gauge transformations. The margin note records the dlog map φ ↦ dφ/φ that makes this quotient.
- The last map is the Atiyah class (dlog Chern class), which is the obstruction to the existence of a connection.

NB. Suppose f is proper and flat and Ω^1 is cohomologically flat in degree 0. Then R^1 f_*Ω^1 commutes with base change and is a vector group. Any homomorphism from an abelian scheme B into it is zero. Hence for any u: B → Pic_{X/S}, the image of B lies in the image of P^c, and pulling back gives (1.2):
0 → f_*Ω^1 → u^*P^c → B → 0.
When Pic^0_{X/S} is an abelian scheme B and u is the inclusion, this gives (1.3):
0 → f_*Ω^1 → (P^c)^0 → Pic^0 → 0.
This sequence is functorial in X/S and compatible with base change.

(2) The page then introduces P^{ci}, the subsheaf of P^c where the connection is integrable (curvature zero). On the next page this is followed by the exact sequence with relative de Rham cohomology, a crystalline replacement in the non-smooth case, and the identification of (P^{ci})^0 with the universal vector extension of Pic^0 = A^∨ when f_*Ω^1_X ≅ f_*Ω^1_{Alb}.

The purpose is to build the object later called Pic^♮ (the universal vector extension) and to relate it to H^1_dR and to one-dimensional crystalline cohomology.
errors: The kernel of P^c → Pic should be f_*Ω^1 / dlog f_*O^*, not f_*Ω^1. Grothendieck notices this in the margin; it reduces to f_*Ω^1 when f_*O_X = O_S universally (proper, geometrically connected fibres), since dlog of a unit coming from S is zero relative to S.

The claim that R^1 f_*Ω^1 commutes with base change needs more than cohomological flatness of Ω^1 in degree 0. One needs local freeness / cohomological flatness in degree 1, or at least representability by a vector group, for Hom(B, R^1) = 0 to follow. This is a minor gap.
Letter slip: 'schéma abélien A' and then 'hom B →'; the same abelian scheme is meant.

ideas.what: Picard functor of line bundles with (integrable) connection, and the exact sequence 0 → f_*Ω^1 → Pic^♮ → Pic → R^1 f_*Ω^1 via the Atiyah class
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (idea), developed by Mazur–Messing 1974 (LNM 370) and Messing 1973; earlier Rosenlicht for curves
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck, 'Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux' (ICM 1970) and the Montréal lectures (1974) treat universal extensions; Mazur–Messing attribute the Pic^♮ construction to him

ideas.what: Line bundles with connection on Pic^0 (abelian scheme) give an extension by f_*Ω^1, which is the universal vector extension of Pic^0
ideas.where_published: Mazur–Messing, 'Universal extensions and one-dimensional crystalline cohomology', LNM 370

ideas.what: Homomorphisms from an abelian scheme to a vector group vanish, which forces line bundles in Pic^0 to admit connections

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of the well-known Pic^♮ / universal vector extension construction, which Mazur–Messing published (and credited to Grothendieck) in 1974. Nothing here goes beyond the literature.
transcription_corrections: Margin reads: 'f^{fl}_*O^*_{X/S} → f^{fl}_*(Ω^1_{X/S}) donné par φ ↦ dφ/φ. Est-ce un hom.? ... une hyp. supplém. propre et plat, de prés. finie, p. ex. projectif lisse'. The arrow under (1.1) indicates that the kernel term should be taken modulo Im f_*(O^*_{X/S}), not Ω^*.
In the NB the abelian scheme is first written 'A' and then 'B'; read uniformly as B.
'(1.2) … → u^*(P^c) → B → 1' (the final term is written as 1, i.e. 0).
